strengths: Clearly identifies and effectively illustrates mean-collapse as a significant failure mode in perturbation prediction with compelling visual evidence (Figure 1)
Technically sound methodology combining semantic and structural embeddings for perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction with appropriate use of Gumbel-Softmax sampling
Comprehensive evaluation with well-chosen complementary metrics: both global (Pearson-∆, PDS) and DEG-aware metrics (DES@K, Spearman, direction-match) that directly address the stated problem
Thorough experimental setup including ablation studies (Figures 4-5), effect-size stratified analysis revealing important regularization insights, and proper held-out perturbation validation
Substantial improvements on DEG recovery metrics: DES@50 improvements of 19-28% over TxPert across datasets, directly confirming the method addresses the stated problem
Extensive documentation with detailed appendices, clear dataset statistics, hyperparameter search spaces, and reproducibility details
weaknesses: Critical circular dependency: method requires ground-truth DEG identification (p<0.05) at training time for loss computation (Eq. 16, 18), conflating training signal with perturbation labels—this fundamental requirement deserves prominent discussion but is underemphasized

Limited novelty: perturbation-conditioned graph scoring, three-component loss design, and Gumbel-Softmax sampling are all standard techniques; contribution is primarily application-focused rather than methodologically novel

Modest improvements on global metrics (Pearson-∆: 6.7% relative on K562, 2.9% on RPE1) lacking statistical significance testing, contradicting claims of substantial improvement; larger gains concentrated in DEG-specific metrics raise questions about generalization

Narrow experimental scope: only 2 cell lines from single dataset (Replogle et al., 2022), only single-gene CRISPR knockouts, no multi-gene or alternative perturbation modalities, no cross-dataset evaluation—limits generalizability claims

Heavy dependence on external proprietary resources (GPT-4o for embeddings, GenePT coverage 95-99%, STRING PPI network requiring arbitrary top-k filtering) with no ablation isolating semantic embedding contribution, threatening reproducibility

Significant hyperparameter sensitivity (λ_non varies dramatically by effect size; Figure 5) with no principled guidance for deployment; practitioners must know effect size a priori or over-tune on validation data

Insufficient failure analysis: single example of pathway validation (HIRA, r=0.53 is moderate not strong), no analysis of perturbations with weak KG proximity, missing simple ablations (DEG-weighted reconstruction alone, structure-only subgraphs)
Limited pathway-level validation: only HIRA knockdown examined with moderate correlation (r=0.53); multi-perturbation pathway analysis needed to validate biological fidelity

strengths: Well-motivated problem: mean collapse is clearly illustrated and acknowledged as a genuine failure mode in genetic perturbation prediction

Comprehensive experimental validation across four datasets with multiple metrics (global, DEG-aware, pathway-level) and thorough ablations including effect-size stratification and hyperparameter sensitivity analysis
Targeted improvements where most needed: 28% DES improvement for small-effect perturbations (<5% DEGs), the regime where mean collapse is most severe
Biologically grounded evaluation: pathway enrichment analysis demonstrates improvements translate to meaningful biological signals beyond metric optimization
Clear methodology presentation: effective figures (2-3) and clear problem decomposition (Eq. 4) that motivates the adaptive learning scheme
Thoughtful technical design: semantic embeddings complement structural graph information, Huber loss balances noise sensitivity, perturbation-specific subgraph extraction is well-motivated
weaknesses: Improvements over strong baseline (TxPert) are incremental: ~5.5% on K562 Pearson-Δ, ~3.2% on RPE1, and underperformance in cross-cell-line setting (0.460 vs Linear 0.515), limiting significance for ICML standards

Circular dependency on DEG definitions: DEGs identified via statistical testing are used both during training (Lalign loss) and evaluation, creating a potential data leakage concern despite robustness checks in Appendix D

Methodological complexity without full justification: six key hyperparameters with unclear selection procedures; multiple loss terms interact in non-obvious ways (e.g., λnon shows effect-size-dependent behavior in Figure 5 without clear explanation); no principled justification for three-loss design vs alternatives

Reproducibility and external dependency concerns: no code availability mentioned, relies on proprietary OpenAI APIs (text embeddings/GPT-4o), no discussion of computational costs or wall-clock time comparisons, hyperparameter tuning procedures not fully documented

Limited scope and generalization: evaluation restricted to single-cell CRISPR from one experimental platform (Replogle et al.); no evaluation on multi-gene perturbations, drug perturbations, or other cell types; cross-cell-line results show limitations; some pathways remain hard (Figure 27)

Incomplete technical documentation: projection head g(·) architecture unspecified, Huber loss threshold δ selection vague, no justification for cosine similarity in Eq. 20, Gumbel-softmax temperature τ selection not motivated
Semantic embedding design: pre-trained OpenAI embeddings capture general knowledge but may not represent perturbation-specific information well; no exploration of jointly learning embeddings

Statistical rigor gaps: no significance tests between methods, single train/val/test split per dataset without cross-validation, limited ablation on core design choices (why three losses, not two or four?)

strengths: Clear problem identification: Mean collapse is well-articulated with convincing empirical evidence (Figure 1)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Four datasets, multiple metrics (global + DEG-aware), extensive ablations and sensitivity analyses
Technically sound approach: Sensible combination of structural embeddings, semantic embeddings, and sparse node selection via Gumbel-Softmax
Thorough appendix: DEG threshold sensitivity (Section D), knowledge graph variants (Section E), attention threshold analysis (Section F) strengthen reproducibility
Honest limitations discussion: Acknowledges need for experimental validation and appropriately cautious impact statement
weaknesses: Critical dependency on ground-truth DEG labels: Training requires knowing which genes are responsive (for L_non and L_align), severely limiting practical applicability to truly unseen perturbations in new cell types/organisms. This makes the contribution somewhat circular—using known response patterns to train a response predictor.

Modest performance improvements on global metrics: Only 6.7% relative improvement on Pearson-Δ (primary metric) vs. TxPert. Larger gains are only on DEG-specific metrics that rely on ground-truth labels. No statistical significance testing provided.

Limited technical novelty: Primarily combines existing techniques (GNNs, language model embeddings, Gumbel-Softmax, multi-loss training). Novelty is in application rather than methodology—below the bar for ICML.

Weak cross-cell-line generalization: Figure 13 shows ADAPERT (0.460) underperforms Linear-GenePT baseline (0.515) in cross-cell-line setting, suggesting the adaptive subgraph mechanism may not be the key factor and generalization is limited.

Technical details underspecified: Huber loss threshold δ formula not provided; Gumbel-Softmax temperature τ not discussed; projection head g(·) architecture missing; unclear if baseline hyperparameters were equally optimized.
Proprietary API dependency: OpenAI embeddings required, raising reproducibility concerns if API changes. Introduces commercial lock-in to an academic method.
Narrow experimental scope: Single-cell perturbations only, single-gene knockdowns only, no bulk RNA-seq or combination perturbations. All experiments on human cell lines.

DEG label circularity: Section D shows robustness to threshold definitions, but doesn't address fundamental issue that alignment loss directly supervises subgraph to match known DEG signals—this is supervised signal recovery, not unsupervised sparsity discovery.

strengths: Clear identification and demonstration of mean collapse as a critical failure mode in perturbation prediction
Technically sound methodology combining perturbation-conditioned subgraph extraction with multi-objective adaptive learning
Comprehensive and rigorous experimental validation across 4 cell lines with both global and DEG-aware metrics
Particularly strong improvements on biologically relevant metrics (DES@50: +20% on K562; +28% improvement for small-effect perturbations)
Extensive ablation studies examining knowledge graph sources, edge density, context extraction methods, and attention thresholds
Practical impact for drug discovery, especially for weak/small-effect perturbations where mean collapse is most severe
Excellent supplementary material with detailed data statistics, pathway-level validation, and multiple evaluation protocols
Improved perturbation discrimination (PDS) not just correlation, addressing the core problem
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: combines standard techniques (Gumbel-Softmax, Huber loss, multi-task learning, text embeddings) without significant methodological innovation

Problematic train-test mismatch with DEG supervision: non-DEG loss and alignment loss use ground-truth DEGs from training data, but paper doesn't clearly explain how DEGs are identified for unseen test perturbations
Concerning cross-cell-line generalization (Figure 13): Linear-GenePT achieves 0.515 Pearson-Δ vs ADAPERT's 0.460, contradicting generalization claims and suggesting cell-line overfitting
Heavy knowledge graph dependency: restricted to genes in STRING PPI, inapplicable to rare/novel genes or multi-gene perturbations; performance heavily dependent on graph quality
Modest absolute improvements in many cases (5-10%, often overlapping with baseline standard deviations); PDS actually decreases on RPE1 (0.618→0.663)
Missing computational cost analysis: no discussion of training time, memory usage, or inference latency compared to baselines
Insufficient interpretability analysis: limited visualization of learned subgraphs vs regulatory relationships; no analysis of what structural properties predict subgraph composition
Incomplete statistical rigor: no formal significance tests, no multiple comparison corrections; some improvements may be within noise
Pathway analysis shows modest correlation (r=0.53 for HIRA case study) and some pathways show negative correlations across all methods
Incomplete engagement with recent LLM-based methods beyond GenePT embeddings; missing comparisons with scGenePT, domain-specific models, or other adaptive graph approaches
